lessons.title: Many Festivals, Many Friends
objectives: Name several festivals celebrated in India
Describe one way each is celebrated
explanation: Festivals are special days when people celebrate together. In India, people of many religions and regions celebrate many festivals.

Diwali is a festival of lights with diyas and sweets. Eid al-Fitr comes after the month of Ramadan, with prayers, sheer khurma and visiting family. Christmas celebrates the birth of Jesus with carols and a decorated tree. Gurpurab celebrates the Sikh Gurus. Holi is a spring festival of colours.
We can wish friends on their festivals: "Happy Diwali!", "Eid Mubarak!", "Merry Christmas!" Sharing joy makes everyone feel welcome.

context.text: Each festival has religious meaning for those who celebrate it; for example, Christians celebrate Christmas as the birth of Jesus, and Sikhs celebrate Gurpurab to honour the Gurus.
Many families also have their own festival customs passed down through generations.

prerequisites: Knows their own family food and clothes
explanation: India is a big country with many regions. People in different places eat different foods: idli and dosa are popular in the south, poha in Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh, makki roti in Punjab, fish and rice in Bengal and Kerala.
Clothes are different too: saris worn in many styles, kurtas, dhotis, salwar kameez, and special clothes for festivals and weddings.
These differences are what make India colourful. All of them are part of being Indian.

context.text: Regional foods and dress styles have developed over centuries, shaped by climate, crops and local traditions; many are now enjoyed across the country.

lessons.title: Why Do We Celebrate?
objectives: Retell the traditional story or meaning of several festivals
Recognise that one festival can have different stories in different regions
explanation: Many festivals remember important stories. In many parts of North India, Diwali celebrates Rama's return to Ayodhya; in other places it honours Lakshmi, or Krishna's victory over Narakasura; Jains mark it as Mahavira's nirvana, and Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas.

Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan, a month of fasting, prayer and charity for Muslims. Christmas celebrates the birth of Jesus for Christians. Buddha Purnima remembers the birth, enlightenment and passing of the Buddha. Mahavir Jayanti celebrates the birth of Mahavira.
So one festival can carry different stories, and different festivals share values like light, kindness, charity and family.

context.text: The stories connected with festivals are traditional narratives, told and understood in different ways across communities and regions.
For followers, these festivals have religious significance, such as Ramadan as a month of fasting commanded in Islam.

lessons.title: Thank You, Harvest!
objectives: Name harvest festivals from different regions
Explain why farming communities celebrate harvests
explanation: For farming communities, a good harvest means food for the year. Many festivals celebrate the harvest and give thanks.

In mid-January, around the Sun's shift towards the north, people celebrate Pongal in Tamil Nadu, Makar Sankranti across many states, Lohri in Punjab and Magh Bihu in Assam. Onam in Kerala and Baisakhi in Punjab are other harvest-time festivals.
Harvest festivals often include cooking the first rice, bonfires, kite flying, dancing and sharing food. Many countries have similar festivals, like Thanksgiving.

context.text: Pongal is named after a dish of newly harvested rice boiled with milk and jaggery; families let it boil over as a sign of abundance.
Makar Sankranti is one of the few Indian festivals tied to the solar calendar, so it falls on about the same date (14 or 15 January) each year.

lessons.title: Namaste, Vanakkam, Sat Sri Akal
objectives: Name several Indian languages and their scripts
Use greetings in different languages
explanation: India has hundreds of languages. The Constitution's Eighth Schedule lists 22 languages, including Hindi, Marathi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Gujarati, Punjabi, Odia, Urdu, Assamese and Sanskrit.
Languages use different scripts. Hindi, Marathi and Sanskrit use Devanagari. Tamil, Bengali, Gurmukhi (for Punjabi) and the Urdu script (written right to left) look very different.
Greetings change too: namaste or namaskar, vanakkam (Tamil), sat sri akal (Punjabi), as-salamu alaykum or adaab, nomoshkar (Bengali). Learning a greeting is a way to show respect.

context.text: The Eighth Schedule of the Constitution of India lists 22 languages; the Census records many more mother tongues.
Greetings often carry cultural or religious meaning; for example, "Sat Sri Akal" is a Sikh greeting meaning "Truth is the timeless Lord".

lessons.title: Painting Traditions
objectives: Identify several Indian folk art styles
Explain how homes suit their climate and materials
explanation: India has many folk painting traditions. Warli art from Maharashtra uses simple white shapes — circles, triangles and lines — to show daily life. Madhubani (Mithila) art from Bihar uses bold lines and bright colours filled with patterns. Gond art from Madhya Pradesh uses dots and lines to bring animals and trees to life.
These arts were often painted on walls and floors for festivals and weddings, and many are now painted on paper and cloth too.

Traditional homes suit their environment: houses on stilts in flood-prone Assam, thick mud walls that stay cool in Rajasthan, sloping roofs for heavy rain in Kerala, and houseboats on Kashmir's lakes.

context.text: Folk art styles are passed down within communities, such as the Warli people of Maharashtra and Mithila women in Bihar; many themes come from local traditions and beliefs.

lessons.title: Celebrations Across the World
objectives: Describe festivals from several countries
Compare them with Indian festivals
explanation: Around the world, people celebrate with lights, food, family and music. Lunar New Year, celebrated in China and many East Asian communities, features red decorations, dumplings and dragon dances.

Hanukkah is the Jewish festival of lights, when families light a menorah for eight nights. Nowruz, the Persian New Year at the spring equinox, is celebrated in Iran and Central Asia — and by Parsi communities in India. Día de los Muertos in Mexico honours family members who have died, with flowers and altars.
Comparing festivals shows both differences and shared human themes: new beginnings, remembering ancestors, light over darkness and gratitude.

context.text: Hanukkah commemorates, in Jewish tradition, the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem and the miracle of the oil lasting eight days.
Día de los Muertos blends Indigenous Mexican and Catholic traditions.

lessons.title: The Chilli's Journey
objectives: Give examples of cultural exchange through trade
Recognise and avoid cultural stereotypes
explanation: Cultures have always exchanged ideas, goods and foods. Chillies, tomatoes and potatoes — now central to Indian cooking — came from the Americas and reached India after the 1500s, largely through Portuguese trade.
Indian spices, textiles, mathematics (like the decimal place-value system with zero) and stories travelled the other way, along sea routes and the Silk Road.
A stereotype is an oversimplified idea about a group ("everyone from X is Y"). Real understanding means learning from people themselves and recognising that every culture contains great variety.

context.text: Historians trace the introduction of chillies to India to the Portuguese in the 16th century; the Hindu–Arabic numeral system spread from India to the Islamic world and then to Europe.

lessons.title: The Culture Iceberg
objectives: Distinguish visible and less visible aspects of culture
Reflect on their own multiple identities
explanation: Culture is the shared way of life of a group: language, food, dress, arts, festivals, beliefs, values and ways of behaving.

The "culture iceberg" image shows that some parts are easy to see (food, clothing, festivals) while bigger parts lie below the surface (values, ideas of respect, family roles, ideas about time and communication).
Each person belongs to many groups — family, region, language, religion or none, school, interests — so identity is layered. Respecting others means being curious about their whole iceberg.

context.text: The iceberg model is a teaching metaphor used in intercultural education; it simplifies how culture works.

lessons.title: India's World Heritage
objectives: Describe tangible and intangible heritage
Discuss threats to heritage and how to protect it
explanation: Heritage is what we inherit from the past and want to pass on. Tangible heritage includes monuments and places, like the Ajanta and Ellora caves, the Taj Mahal, Hampi and the Sun Temple at Konark — all UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
Intangible heritage includes living traditions: Yoga, Kumbh Mela, Durga Puja in Kolkata, Ramlila, Garba of Gujarat and Vedic chanting are on UNESCO's intangible heritage lists.
Heritage faces threats: pollution, unplanned tourism, neglect and climate change. Protecting it requires careful conservation, responsible tourism and community involvement.

context.text: UNESCO has inscribed over 40 sites in India on the World Heritage List; Durga Puja in Kolkata was added to the intangible cultural heritage list in 2021 and Garba in 2023.

lessons.title: Seeing From the Inside
objectives: Explain ethnocentrism and cultural relativism
Describe anthropological methods and ethics
explanation: Ethnocentrism means judging other cultures by the standards of your own, often assuming your own is "normal" or superior. Cultural relativism means trying to understand practices in their own context before judging.
Anthropologists use participant observation: living with a community, learning its language and taking part in daily life, while recording carefully.

Ethics matter: informed consent, respecting privacy, avoiding harm, and sharing benefits with communities. Relativism doesn't mean accepting everything — human rights provide shared standards — but it encourages understanding before judging.

context.text: Scholars debate how to balance cultural relativism with universal human rights; this lesson presents that debate rather than resolving it.

vocabulary.meaning: judging other cultures by your own standards

examples: Assuming eating with hands is "messy" is ethnocentric.

After living there for a week, learning about forest materials and climate, she rewrote her notes: "Homes are built from local bamboo and mud, cool in summer and easy to repair." Understanding had changed her words.

lessons.title: Unity in Diversity
objectives: Analyse religious and cultural pluralism in India
Evaluate effects of globalisation on culture
explanation: India is home to followers of Hinduism, Islam, Christianity, Sikhism, Buddhism, Jainism, Zoroastrianism, Judaism, tribal religions and people of no religion. The Constitution guarantees freedom of religion and describes India as a secular state, treating all religions with equal respect.

Indian history includes syncretic traditions that blended ideas: Bhakti saints like Kabir and Sufi saints like Nizamuddin Auliya drew followers across communities; Hindustani classical music grew from many influences.

Globalisation spreads films, foods, brands and ideas worldwide. It can bring opportunity and creative mixing, but some worry about loss of local languages and traditions. Communities respond by adapting, reviving and sharing their cultures.

context.text: The word "secular" was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment in 1976; Articles 25–28 guarantee freedom of religion.
Followers of each tradition understand their beliefs in their own terms; teachings of saints like Kabir and Nizamuddin Auliya are revered by their followers.
Scholars and citizens debate the meaning and practice of secularism in India.

vocabulary.meaning: many groups living together with mutual respect
not favouring any religion
blending different traditions
increasing worldwide connections

examples: Ajmer Sharif dargah visited by people of many faiths.

story.title: Kabir's Couplets
story.text: In the 15th century, the poet-saint Kabir wrote simple couplets (dohas) questioning empty rituals and celebrating devotion. Both Hindus and Muslims claimed him. Today, his verses are sung by folk singers in villages, quoted in schools and set to music in films — a voice still crossing boundaries.

project.title: Pluralism Case Study
steps: Choose a syncretic tradition, shared shrine or multicultural neighbourhood
Research its history and present practice
Interview community members if possible
Write a report on how diversity is lived there
project.safety: Obtain consent before interviews, explain the purpose, and respect requests not to answer. Do not identify participants or present one person's views as representing an entire community.
